summary:
Across 13 evals (24 iterations), 2 were skipped as not applicable (should_trigger: false cases, both correctly did not fire — not a quality signal either way) and 11 chat evals were compared in depth.

**Expected-output match:** In 9 of the 11 scored evals, without_skill failed to meet the expected output (0/1) while with_skill met it (1/1): api-key-inventory, scp-impact-before-applying, no-guardrail-on-production-path, draft-not-pinned-trap, blocked-sometimes-no-account, version-limit-counts-draft, pii-entry-with-only-action, invocation-log-input-assessment-is-not-detection. In the remaining 2 (bpa-dormant-keys, gr-prompt-attack, gr-no-apply) both variants met the expected output. Confidence on these expected-output judgments is mostly "high" or "medium," so this is a fairly firm pattern, not a borderline call, though it rests on LLM judgment rather than hard ground truth.

**Assertion pass rates:** Following the same pattern, with_skill scored at or near 100% assertion pass rate in nearly every eval, while without_skill trailed noticeably in most (e.g., 27% vs 91% on api-key-inventory, 62% vs 100% on scp-impact-before-applying, 57% vs 100% on pii-entry-with-only-action, 69% vs 100% on invocation-log-input-assessment, 57% vs 100% on version-limit-counts-draft). On bpa-dormant-keys, gr-prompt-attack, and gr-no-apply the gap was smaller (with_skill slightly ahead: 80 vs 60, 83 vs 67, 83 vs 67). Several assertions reveal recurring, specific without_skill weaknesses: not disclaiming read-only/no-changes behavior, missing AWS documentation links, exposing 12-digit account numbers or full key IDs in some evals, and not labeling inferences as observations rather than documented behavior. Some assertions passed for both variants (e.g., resolving which guardrail version applies, identifying ML-based guardrails as probabilistic) and some failed for both (e.g., "treats expired key as non-reenableable," "specific resource named" in gr-prompt-attack, "GRD catalog check-id" in gr-no-apply) — these point to assertion/behavior gaps that apply regardless of variant, not a between-variant difference.

**Mixed/counter-pattern result:** In bpa-dormant-keys, one assertion ("staged deactivate-before-delete sequence") favored without_skill over with_skill, and without_skill avoided exposing full key identifiers/account IDs in that eval better than with_skill failed it — so the general pattern is not universal; there are cases/assertions where without_skill did as well or better.

**Runtime and cost:** No consistent direction. with_skill was slower/costlier in several evals (api-key-inventory: 1m56s/$0.97 vs 59s/$0.49; bpa-dormant-keys: 1m38s/$0.82 vs 42s/$0.35; gr-prompt-attack: 1m25s/$0.71 vs 20s/$0.17), but without_skill was slower/costlier in scp-impact-before-applying (4m5s/$2.03 vs 2m11s/$1.09) and invocation-log-input-assessment (25s/$0.21 for with_skill vs 11s/$0.09, i.e. without_skill cheaper there too). draft-not-pinned-trap shows without_skill at 0s/$0.01, suggesting a possible non-response or very truncated run, paired with all of without_skill's assertions coming back "inconclusive" (no data) for that eval. Context-window utilization was consistently a bit higher for with_skill, though both stayed low overall (under ~12%).

**Quality comparisons:** Head-to-head quality judgments were only run for 4 of the 11 evals (bpa-dormant-keys, gr-prompt-attack, gr-no-apply) with pairs_evaluated=1 each and medium/high confidence; the rest were skipped (pairs_skipped=1, no comparable pairs). Where comparisons ran, with_skill was favored overall in bpa-dormant-keys (favored on actionability, tied on accuracy/completeness) and gr-prompt-attack (favored on all three criteria), while gr-no-apply was split (without_skill favored on accuracy, with_skill on completeness, tied on actionability) — indicating a close or mixed quality result in that one case despite with_skill's edge elsewhere. Given the very small number of evaluated pairs, these quality comparisons rest on thin data.

**Consistency:** No output-consistency data was available for either variant in any eval (all null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this report.

**Overall picture:** Variant_b met the expected output and passed assertions more often across most evals, often by a wide margin, and was favored in the few head-to-head quality comparisons that were run. Variant_a was occasionally faster/cheaper and in isolated cases (bpa-dormant-keys's staged-deletion assertion, gr-no-apply's accuracy criterion) performed as well or better. The draft-not-pinned-trap eval for without_skill returned no usable data (0s runtime, inconclusive assertions), which should be treated as a data gap rather than evidence either way. Two evals were correctly skipped as not applicable to either variant. Confidence in the expected-output and assertion judgments is generally medium-to-high, but the quality-comparison dataset is sparse (only 3 of 11 evals had any head-to-head quality pairs), and consistency data is entirely absent, so some dimensions of this evaluation remain thin.

api-key-inventory.summary:
Both variants had the trigger fire (1/1), so the behavior under test was exercised in both cases.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output (1/1, medium confidence), while without_skill did not (0/1, high confidence). The high confidence on without_skill's failure means this is a fairly solid finding rather than a borderline judgment call.

Assertions (11 total per variant): with_skill passed 10/11 (91%), without_skill passed 3/11 (27%). Breaking this down:
- Three assertions passed for both variants (listing all API keys found; stating IAM doesn't report last-used so usage status is unknown; stating the audit was read-only with no changes made). These are not distinguishing factors since both variants satisfy them.
- One assertion failed for both variants (treating expired keys as non-reactivatable vs. inactive keys as reactivatable) — this suggests either the assertion or the underlying agent behavior needs attention regardless of variant.
- Seven assertions passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill: explaining each key's grant/risk tier and removal steps, stating IAM doesn't report key last-used, never printing full key IDs or related identifiers, not ending with a follow-up question/offer, citing AWS documentation links, avoiding 12-digit account numbers, and not exposing full access key IDs. Several of these touch on security-sensitive disclosure practices (key IDs, account numbers), so this is a meaningful cluster of differences, not an isolated metric.

Metrics: with_skill took longer on average (1m56s vs 59s, roughly double) and cost more (~$0.97 vs ~$0.49, also roughly double), with somewhat higher context window utilization (7.1% vs 4.8%, both low, no compaction for either). Given with_skill also showed higher assertion pass rates and met the expected output, this is a case where the slower/costlier variant also produced more complete and compliant output — a tradeoff rather than a clear regression in either direction, though the quality differential here is large relative to the runtime/cost differential.

Quality comparison and output consistency: no usable data. The quality comparison had 0 pairs evaluated and 1 pair skipped, and output consistency was not computed (null) for either variant, so neither of these dimensions can inform the assessment — this is an absence of data, not a neutral or negative result for either variant.

Overall, this is based on a single task instance, so findings should be treated as a single data point rather than a robust trend. Within that instance, with_skill showed higher assertion compliance and met the expected output while without_skill did not, particularly around sensitive-data handling (key IDs, account numbers) and response completeness (grant/risk explanation, documentation citation, not ending with a follow-up question). Variant_b ran faster and cheaper. One assertion (expired vs. inactive key handling) failed for both, indicating a shared gap unrelated to the variant difference.

- 5 assertions passed for both variants: naming the users with active Bedrock-invoking credentials, stating IAM roles/Identity Center users are unaffected, noting the audit doesn't evaluate existing SCPs/RCPs, not ending with an offer/follow-up question, and not exposing full key IDs. These are not differentiators since both variants handled them correctly.

These three failures for without_skill suggest it may have overstepped by implying action was taken, omitted documentation citations, and leaked a 12-digit number (e.g., an account ID), which are meaningful gaps tied directly to the overall expected-output failure.

These runtime/cost differences favor with_skill, and combined with the assertion/expected-output gaps, there's no quality-for-cost tradeoff evident here — without_skill did not show higher quality to offset its longer runtime and higher cost.

Quality comparison and consistency: No direct quality-comparison pairs were evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so no paired quality judgment is available. Output consistency across repeated runs was not measured (null) for both variants, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed for either.

Overall, this is a single-task eval with high-confidence results showing with_skill passing all assertions and meeting the expected output, while without_skill failed the expected-output check and failed 3 of 8 assertions (notably around overstating actions taken, missing documentation citation, and exposing a 12-digit number), and also took longer and cost more. This evaluation covers a single chat task about reviewing IAM credentials (dormancy, safe-removal guidance, and sensitive data handling). The behavior under test fired as expected (1/1), and both variants met the overall expected output (1/1, medium confidence for both) — so at the top-level outcome, there is no observed difference.

Looking below that aggregate, the picture is mixed. Of 5 assertions, with_skill passed 4/5 (80%) and without_skill passed 3/5 (60%), but the pattern is not one-sided:
- Two assertions passed for both variants (reporting last-used evidence instead of asserting dormancy, and distinguishing "dormant" from "safe to remove") — these don't differentiate the variants.
- One assertion (staged removal sequence / not recommending deletion of actively-used credentials) passed for without_skill but failed for with_skill.
- Two assertions (not writing full key identifiers; not exposing a raw 12-digit account ID) passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill.
So each variant has a distinct weakness: without_skill struggled with masking sensitive identifiers (key IDs, account ID), while with_skill struggled with safe-removal sequencing guidance. These are meaningful, concrete failures on opposite assertions rather than a uniform quality gap.

On the single quality comparison pair available, with_skill was favored overall (actionability favored with_skill; accuracy and completeness were rated comparable), at medium confidence — this is based on only one pair, so it's a thin signal.

For cost and runtime, without_skill was substantially faster (42s vs 1m38s) and cheaper ($0.35 vs $0.82), with lower context-window utilization (4.7% vs 7.9%); neither had any compaction events. The single runtime comparison pair exceeded the 30s threshold, consistent with both variants' runtimes being longer than that threshold. Given with_skill's higher assertion pass rate and favored quality rating, this runtime/cost difference reads as a tradeoff rather than a clear regression for either side.

Output consistency across repeated runs was not available for either variant (both null), so stability across runs cannot be assessed here.

Overall, this is based on a single task/pair, limiting confidence in any pattern. The two variants show complementary, specific weaknesses (sensitive-data masking vs. removal-sequencing guidance) rather than one variant being uniformly stronger, while without_skill is faster and cheaper and with_skill scored slightly higher on assertions and was favored in the one quality comparison.
